surveys.narrative: Walleye, perch and tullibee were taken in above average numbers. Smallmouth bass, sucker, and rock bass were taken in average numbers. Northern pike and crappie were taken in below average numbers. 80% of the walleyes are age I-IV. Good reproduction is evident in most years. Growth on walleyes is somewhat slower than for other walleye lakes in the Ely area. The walleye population and growth rates are quite similar to past assessments and surveys, although it appears that since 1941 the long term trend has been towards younger and smaller fish in Lake Vermilion. Composed of above average populations of walleye, tullibee, and yellow perch. Sucker, smallmouth bass, and rock bass are present in about average numbers. Northern pike, bluegill, and crappies are present in below average numbers. 80% of the walleyes are age I-IV. Walleye reproduction appears to be more variable on west vermilion than east vermilion, although it appears that at least some occurs each year. Growth rates are somewhat faster than on east vermilion. The long term trend shows that the walleye population is moving towards younger and smaller fish.

This trapnet assessment shows above average populations of northern, yellow perch, walleye and rock bass, sucker, bluegill, and crappie were taken in average numbers. Bullheads and smallmouth bass were taken in below average numbers. The bluegill and crappies appear to be above average in size. The smallmouth and largemouth bass populations are quite a bit lower than was expected and are much lower than the populations in west vermilion. This trap net assessment shows above average populations of northern pike, yellow perch, walleye, bluegill and rock bass. Largemouth bass, smallmouth bass and crappies are present in about average numbers while suckers are present in low numbers. The bass appear to be smaller than average and the panfish are about average in size.

Walleye, yellow perch and tullibee were taken in above average numbers. White sucker, northern pike and bluegill and rock bass were taken in average numbers. Smallmouth bass and black crappie were taken in below average numbers. 79% of the walleye are age I-IV.

The 1986 gill netting shows the walleye population both in terms of numbers/lift and pds/lift, to be below the mean observed since 1941, but still above the statewide average and within limits of normal short term fluctuation. Strong year classes are from 1980 and 1983. 1982 appears to be particularly weak year class and is probably responsible for the decreased catch rate. The northern pike catch was very low, as it historically always has been. The average size, however, is quite large, mean tl 28.3 21.4/gillnet is above the statewide median, but about equal to the historical average for vermilion. The yellow perch population in vermilion has been historically stable. The northern cisco catch of 15.0/lift is very close to the historical average of 12.5/lift and is quite a bit higher than the statewide median.

The walleye gillnet catch in 1987 of 11.2 fish per set is near the long term average of 12.0 per set for lake vermilion. The catch remains well above state and local medians. The average size of captured walleye is relatively small, which is typical for Lake Vermilion. The northern pike gill net catch in 1987 (0.5 fish/set) was below state and local medians, which is normal for Lake Vermilion. Since the inception of large lake assessment work in 1984, the northern pike catch has been very consistent, at 0.6 or 0.5 fish per set.

The walleye gillnet catch in 1988 of 12.4 fish per net is near the long term average for Lake Vermilion and is well above state and local medians. The walleye population in Lake Vermilion has been relatively stable since the 1940's. The average length of gillnetted walleye was 13 is near the historical average. The northern pike gillnet catch in 1988 was 0.9 fish per net, slightly higher than recent years. The northern pike population in Lake Vermilion has typically been relatively low numbers of relatively large fish. The gillnet catch of northern cisco and yellow perch was down slightly from recent years but still above state and local medians. Gillnet catches of other major species in Lake Vermilion were close to historical averages. Centrarchid population remain at a relatively high level in lake vermilion. The trapnet catch of bluegill in 1988 was 39.2 fish per net. This is down from 56.4 fish per net in 1987, probably reflecting a decline in influence of a very strong 1983 year class. Bluegill, are a recent addition to the fish community in Lake Vermilion, first reported in the lake in 1970. Pumpkinseed and black crappie are present in Lake Vermilion in lower numbers than bluegill, with a trapnet catch in 1988 of 4.9 fish per net and 1.9 fish per set, respectively. Black crappie numbers have been relatively stable in recent years while pumpkinseed numbers appear to be increasing.

The walleye population in Lake Vermilion remains at a relatively high level. The 1989 walleye gill- net catch of 13.5 fish/lift is slightly above the long term average from Lake Vermilion and is well above the state and local medians. The average length of gillnetted walleye was 13.2 higher than the historical average. The northern pike gillnet catch in 1989 was 1.4 fish/lift, slightly higher than recent years. Historically, the northern pike population in lake vermilion has consisted of relatively low numbers of relatively large fish. The gillnet catch of norther cisco has rebounded somewhat from relatively low catches in 1987 and 1988. The gillnet catch is now close to the historical average for Lake Vermilion and well above state and local medians. Yellow perch remain very abundant in Lake Vermilion. The catch is slightly above the long term average and is well above state and local medians. Bullheads numbers are apparently increasing in lake vermilion. Anglers reported catching many more bullheads in 1989 than in any previous year. The apparent increase is not reflected in the gillnet catch of although the trapnet catch has been increasing since 1987.

The walleye population in Lake Vermilion remains at a relatively high level. The 1990 gillnet catch of 15.5 fish/lift is the third highest on record and continues a trend of 4 consecutive years of increasing gillnet catches. The mean length of gillnetted walleye in 1990 was 12.7 than the historical mean. The yellow perch population is also currently at a high level with a gillnet catch of 33.4 fish/lift, the third highest on record. The gillnet catch of northern pike (1.2 fish/lift) is the same as the historical mean for Lake Vermilion. Historically, the northern pike population on Lake Vermilion has been very stable at a relatively low level. The gillnet catch of cisco in 1990 was 10.6 fish/lift, which is near the historical average of 11.9 fish/lift. The cisco population has apparently recovered from relatively low levels in 1987 and 1988. The bluegill trapnet catch in 1990 (17.3 fish/lift) was about half the catch in 1989 (36.6 fish/lift). It is doubtful the decline in the trapnet catch represents a similar decline in the actual bluegill population. Anglers and resorts reported as many bluegill caught as in the previous several years. Trapnet catches of bluegill have, however, been in a general downward trend since 1987, when the catch was 56.4 fish/lift. Other species sampled in Lake Vermilion are present in relatively low numbers with relatively stable populations.

The 1993 walleye gill net catch was the lowest observed since 1987 and was slightly below the long term median for the lake. The walleye catch was still well within the third quartile for all Class 2 lakes. The decline in the walleye catch was primarily due to the lack of strong, younger year classes. The last strong year class was produced in 1988 and the influence of that year class is now declining. The 1993 walleye catch was dominated by relatively average 1990 and 1991 year classes. Poor growth of young-of-the-year walleye in 1992 and 1993 indicates these year classes may be average to below average as well.The yellow perch population remains at high level, well above average for Lake Vermilion and other Class 2 lakes. Perch numbers have been relatively high since 1989. The bluegill population has stabilized at a relatively moderate level in recent years after an exceptionally high level in the late 1980's. Black crappie numbers are slightly below average, primarily because no strong year classes have been produced since 1987. Population levels of the other major species sampled are near historical averages.

The 1994 walleye gill net catch was the lowest since since the Large Lake Sampling program began in 1984. It was the second consectutive year of relatively low walleye catches. Although the walleye catch was low for Lake Vermilion, it was still well within the normal range for all Class 2 lakes. The decline in the walleye catch was due primarily to the lack of strong younger year classes. The last strong year class was produced in 1988 and the influence of that year class is now declining. The walleye catch was dominated by the 1991 year class, which is slightly above average, and an average 1990 year class. Catches of the 1992 and 1993 year classes were well below average and it appears these year classes will be weaker than average. Most of the walleye sampled by gill nets were 11 to 14 inches long with a mean length of 13.0 inches. The mean length of young-of-the-year walleye sampled by seining and electrofishing was above average, indicating the 1994 year class has the potential to be stronger than average.The northern pike gill net catch was near average for Lake Vermilion and within the normal range for all Class 2 lakes. Historically, the northern pike population has been very consistent at a level near or slightly below normal for Class 2 lakes. Most of the northern pike sampled were 22 to 28 inches long with a mean length of 24.5 inches. All age classes to age age 8 were represented in the gill net catch.The yellow perch catch declined to a level near normal for Lake Vermilion, after several years of above average catches. Perch catches on Lake Vermilion are typically well above average for Class 2 lakes. Most of the sampled perch were 5 to 7 inches long with a mean length of 6.6 inches. The catch was dominated by the 1992 year class, although all age classes to age 8 were well represented.The bluegill trap net catch was near average for Lake Vermilion and continues a trend of moderate catches that started in 1990, after a period of exceptionally high catches in the late 1980's. Most of the sampled bluegill were 5.5 to 7.5 inches long with a mean length of 6.5 inches. The catch was dominated by a strong 1988 year class. The black crappie catch was below average for Lake Vermilion. It was the second consectutive year of below average crappie catches. The recent decline in the crappie population was due to poor reproduction since 1987, the last year a strong year class was produced. Most of the crappie sampled were 8 to 13 inches long with a mean length of 9.9 inches. The catch was dominated by the 1987 and 1991 year classes.Catches of other species were near their respective historical average.

The walleye gillnet catch in 1995 was 12.4 fish/net, which is about average for Lake Vermilion and above average for other similar type lakes. The walleye population was dominated by age 1 fish (1994 year class) and age 4 fish (1991 year class). Walleye from the 1994 year class were 7-10 inches long. Walleye from the strong 1991 year class were primarily 13-16 inches long and will dominate the angler harvest in 1996. Relatively poor year classes of walleye were produced in 1992 and 1993. Beach seining and electrofishing indicate the 1995 year class should be well above average.Trap net and gill net catches of northern pike were both 1.0 fish/net, which are about average for Lake Vermilion and slightly below average for other similar type lakes. Most of the northern pike sampled were 15-24 inches long. The northern pike population on Lake Vermilion has historically been relatively stable without much year to year flucuation.Only one muskellunge was caught during the 1995 assessment, however they are seldom caught in standard assessment netting gear. Muskellunge were not known to be present in Lake Vermilion until a stocking program began in 1985. Spring assessment netting and angler reports indicate the population is doing quite well with the larger fish now nearing 50 inches.The gill net catch of yellow perch was 17.5 fish/net, which is slightly below average for Lake Vermilion and well above average for other similar type lakes. Most of the perch sampled were 6-8 inches long. Perch tend to be larger in the Big Bay area of the lake, where they averaged 9.1 inches long.The bluegill trap net catch was 17.9 fish/net, which is slightly below the historical average for Lake Vermilion and well above average for other similar type lakes. Most of the bluegill sampled were 6-8 inches long. Strong year classes were produced in 1988 and 1991. The bluegill population has stabilized in recent years after being at an exceptionally high level in the late 1980's.The trap catch of black crappie was 0.7 fish/net, which is below average for Lake Vermilion and below average for other similar type lakes. The crappie population has been at a relatively low level since the decline of a strong 1987 year class. Moderately strong year classes were produced in 1991 and 1994. Most of the crappie sampled were either less than 5 inches long or 9-11 inches long. Because smallmouth bass are seldom caught in standard assessment nets, an electrofishing boat is used to sample the smallmouth bass population. The smallmouth bass catch was 17.3 fish/hour of electrofishing, which is below average for Lake Vermilion. Data for comparison to other lakes is not available. Most of the bass sampled were 8-12 inches long.

The walleye gill net catch in 1996 was 13.2 fish/net, which is slightly above average for Lake Vermilion. Most of the walleye sampled were 10-17 inches long. The walleye catch was dominated by strong 1994 and 1995 year classes. Walleye from the strong 1994 year class were primarily 10-13 inches long and will comprise a major portion of the walleye harvest in 1997. As the summer progresses, growth will make 1994 year class walleye increasingly acceptable to anglers. Walleye from the 1991 year class were primarily 14-17 inches and will also comprise a signifigant portion of the walleye harvest. Poor reproduction in 1992 and 1993 means below average numbers of age 4 and 5 walleye will be available to anglers, age classes that usually comprise a major portion of the walleye harvest.The northern pike gill net catch was 1.4 fish/net, which is slightly above average. The northern pike population has been relatively stable over time, without much year to year flucuation. Most of the northern pike sampled were 15-24 inches long, although larger fish are present. A strong 1994 year class means anglers may catch more small northern pike than usual in 1997.No muskie were caught during the 1996 assessment, however they are seldom caught in standard assessment netting gear. A stocking program that started in 1985 has established a muskie population in the lake. Special spring assessments and angler reports indicate the population is doing well, with the larger fish now nearing 50 inches.The gill net catch of yellow perch was 29.7 fish/net, which is about average for Lake Vermilion. The perch population flucuates more over time than most species present in the lake. Most of the perch sampled were 6-8 inches long. Perch tend to be larger in the Big Bay area of the lake, where they averaged 8.2 inches long.The bluegill trap net catch was 20.7 fish/net, slightly below average for Lake Vermilion. The bluegill population has been relatively stable in recent years. Strong year classes were produced in 1991, 1989, and 1988. Most of the bluegill sampled were 6-8 inches long and will provide good angling opportunities in 1997.The trap net catch of black crappie was 1.7 fish/net, slightly above the historical average. Crappie catches were below average from 1993-1995. The population has recovered due to strong 1994 and 1991 year classes. Most of the crappie sampled were 6-8 inches long, although larger fish are present. Anglers may catch more small crappie than average in 1997, due to the strong 1994 year class.Smallmouth bass are sampled with an electrofishing boat, since they are seldom caught in standard assessment nets. The smallmouth bass catch in 1996 was 26.7 fish/hour, which is near the historical average. The catch was dominated by strong 1994 and 1991 year classes. Most of the bass sampled were 6-15 inches long.

The walleye gillnet catch in 1997 was 15.2 fish/net, which is above the historical average for Lake Vermilion. Most of the walleye sampled were 10-16 inches long. The walleye catch was dominated by strong 1994 and 1995 year classes. Most walleye from the strong 1994 year class were 12-15 inches long and they will comprise a major portion of the walleye harvest in 1998. Walleye from the 1995 year class were primarily 10-13 inches long. As the summer progresses, growth will make the 1995 year class increasingly acceptable to anglers. Poor reproduction in 1992 and 1993 means below average numbers of age 5 and 6 walleye will be available to anglers. Most species experienced poor reproduction in 1992 and 1993, probably due to the cool summer weather in those years.The northern pike gillnet catch was 0.8 fish/net, which is near the historical average. Most of the northern pike sampled were 20-25 inches long, although larger fish are present. The gillnet catch was dominated by a strong 1994 year class.The muskie trapnet catch was 0.5 fish/net during a special spring trapnet assessment on East Vermilion. The catch was considerably higher than the 1993 catch of 0.2 fish/net. Most of muskie sampled were 34-43 inches long. The largest individual muskie caught was 46.1 inches long. All year classes from 1987-1991 were well represented in the catch. Muskie were not native to Lake Vermilion, although a signifigant population has been established by a stocking program that began in 1985.The gillnet catch of yellow perch was 24.8 fish/net, which is near the historical average for Lake Vermilion. Most of the perch sampled were 5-9 inches long. Perch tend to be larger in the Big Bay area of the lake, where 47% of the perch sampled were 9 inches or longer. The gillnet catch of perch was dominated by the 1995 and 1994 year classes. The bluegill trapnet catch was 17.7 fish/net, slightly below the historical average. Bluegill catches have been relatively stable in recent years. The bluegill catch was much higher in West Vermilion than in East Vermilion. Most of the bluegill sampled were 6-8 inches long. Strong year classes were produced in 1995, 1994, 1991, 1988, and 1989.The trapnet catch of black crappie 0.4 fish/net, the lowest catch since sampling began in 1987. Crappie numbers have been below average for several years, due to the declining influence of a strong 1987 year class and the lack of strong, younger year classes. Most of the crappie sampled were 6-9 inches long. Fair year classes were produced in 1994 and 1991.Smallmouth bass are sampled with an electrofishing boat, since they are seldom caught in standard assessment nets. The smallmouth bass catch in 1997 was 26.3 fish/hour, which is near the historical average. Most of the bass sampled were 6-14 inches long, although larger fish are present. The smallmouth bass catch was dominated by the 1995, 1994, and 1991 year classes.

The walleye gillnet catch in 1998 was 15.8 fish/net, the highest catch since the Large Lake Program began in 1984. It was the third consectutive year of above average walleye gillnet catches. High walleye catches in recent years were due to strong year classes produced in 1994 and 1995. Walleye from the 1994 year classes were mostly 14-17 inches long. Walleye from the 1995 year class were mostly 12-15 inches long. Beach seining and electrofishing indicate the 1997 and 1998 year classes should be at least average and possibly above average. The northern pike gillnet catch was 1.0 fish/net, which is also the historical average. Northern pike catches have historically been relatively stable with little annual fluctuation. Most of the northern pike sampled were 20-29 inches long, although larger fish are present. The northern pike catch was dominated by strong 1994 and 1995 year classes.The gillnet catch of yellow perch was 28.9 fish/net, which is near the historical average. Most of the perch sampled were 6-8 inches long. Perch tend to be larger in the Big Bay area of the lake, where 42% of the perch caught were 9 inches or longer. The perch catch was dominated by the 1994 and 1996 year classes. The spring trapnet catch of muskie for West Vermilion was 0.2 fish/net, slightly above the 1994 West Vermilion catch. Muskie population assessments are done in different years for East Vermilion and West Vermilion. An assessment was done on East Vermilion in 1997. Most of the muskie sampled were 38-44 inches long. The largest individual muskie caught was 49.2 inches long. All year classes from 1992-1987 were represented in the catch. Muskie were not present in Lake Vermilion until they were first stocked in 1969. An intensive stocking program using Leech Lake strain fingerlings began in 1987. Angler reports indicate the muskie population is doing well with the larger fish now exceeding 50 inches. The bluegill trapnet catch was 33.5 fish/net, slightly above the historical average and the highest catch since 1989. The bluegill catch was much higher in West Vermilion than in East Vermilion. Most of the bluegill sampled were 6-8 inches long. Strong year classes were produced 1994, 1991, 1989, and 1988. It appears the 1995 year class is exceptionally strong. The trapnet catch of black crappie was 3.4 fish/net, the highest catch since trapnet assessments began in 1987. Crappie trapnet catches had been relatively low for several years. Two distinct size classes of crappie were sampled, 0-5 inches and 9-11 inches. The crappie catch was dominated by strong 1995 and 1997 year classes. Smallmouth bass are sampled with an electrofishing boat since they are seldom caught in assessment nets. The smallmouth bass catch in 1998 was 24.8 fish/hour, which is near the historical average. Most of the bass sampled were 6-13 inches long, although larger fish are present. The smallmouth bass catch was dominated by the 1994 and 1995 year classes.

The walleye gillnet catch in 1999 was 16.9 fish/net, the highest catch since the Large Lake Program began in 1984. It was the fourth consectutive year of above average walleye gillnet catches. High walleye catches in recent years were due to strong year classes produced in 1994, 1995, and 1997. The average length of gillnetted walleye was 13.1 inches, slightly above the historical average. Above average numbers of walleye in the 12-16 inch size range were sampled during the assessment, the size range that dominates the walleye harvest on Lake Vermilion.The northern pike gillnet catch was 0.5 fish/net, slightly below the historical average for Lake Vermilion. Northern pike catches have historically been relatively stable with little annual flucation. The average length of gillnetted pike was 28.8 inches, well above the historical average. Northern pike reproduction seems fairly consistent from year to year, although stronger than average year classes were produced 1991 and 1994. Analysis of northern pike size and age was based on a gillnet catch of only 9 fish, a relatively small sample size. The gillnet catch of yellow perch was 28.9 fish/net, which is near the historical average. Perch catches have been relatively stable in recent years, although they have flucuated widely in the past. The average length of gillnetted perch was 8.0 inches, well above the historical average. Perch tend to larger in the Big Bay area of the lake where 52% of the perch sampled were 9 inches or longer. Average to strong year classes of perch were produced in 1997, 1996, 1995, and 1994.The bluegill trapnet catch was 30.5 fish/net, slightly above the historical average. The bluegill catch was much higher in West Vermilion than in East Vermilion. Strong year classes of bluegill were produced in 1997 and 1995. The average length of trapnetted bluegill was 5.2 inches, well below the historical average. High numbers of small bluegill are present in the population from strong 1995 and 1997 year classes. Some large bluegill are present from remnants of strong year classes produced in 1988, 1989, and 1991. The black crappie trapnet catch was 1.5 fish/net, which is near the historical average. Crappie numbers are usually relatively low on Lake Vermilion, although occasional population spikes occur in response to strong year classes. The average length of trapnetted crappie was 7.5 inches, well below the historical average. Moderately strong year classes were produced in 1997, 1995, and 1994.Muskie population assessments are done on Lake Vermilion once every four years for each of the two major lake basins, East Vermilion and West Vermilion. The last muskie population assessments were done in 1997 on East Vermilion and 1998 on West Vermilion. Most of the muskie caught during the 1997 and 1998 assessments were in the 34-47 inch size range. The largest muskie caught during the assessments was 49.2 inches. Muskie were not present in Lake Vermilion until they were first stocked in 1969. An intensive stocking program using Leech Lake strain fingerlings began in 1987. Angler reports indicate the muskie population is doing well with the larger fish now exceeding 50 inches. The walleye gillnet catch in 2000 was 18.2 fish/net, the highest gillnet catch ever observed on Lake Vermilion. It was the fourth consectutive year of above average walleye gillnet catches. High walleye catches in recent years were due to strong year classes produced in 1994, 1995, and 1997. The 1998 year class also appears to be stronger than average. Poor year classes of walleye were produced in 1992 and 1993. Angling prospects for 2001 are very good, with high numbers of walleye present in the 12-16 inch size range. Small walleye from the 1998 year class will recruit to the fishery as the summer progresses. The fall electrofishing catch of young-of-the-year (YOY) walleye was 85.3 fish/hour, well below the historical average for Lake Vermilion. It was the second consectutive year of below average electrofishing catches of YOY walleye. The mean length of YOY walleye sampled by electrofishing was 4.7 inches, also well below the historical average. Mean length of YOY walleye is strongly correlated to eventual year class strength on Lake Vermilion, with fast growing YOY walleye producing strong year classes and poor growing YOY walleye producing weak year classes. Based on this relationship, it is expected the 2000 year class will be weaker then average.The northern pike gillnet catch was 0.6 fish/net, slightly below the historical average for Lake Vermilion. Northern pike gillnet catches have historically been relatively low with little annual flucuation. The sample size of pike caught by gillnets was too small to make strong conclusions about the size and age structure of the population. Seven of the 12 pike sampled by gillnets were over 28 inches long, which is larger than the usual size range of pike sampled. The catch was comprised primarily of fish age 6 and older. Past netting indicated strong year classes were produced in 1991 and 1994. Angling prospects for 2001 are similar to recent years, although there may be more larger fish than usual in the population.The gillnet catch of yellow perch was 36.7 fish/net, well above the historical average. It was the highest perch catch since 1993. The mean length of gillnetted perch was 7.8 inches, well above the historical average. Strong to average year classes of perch were produced in 1998, 1997, 1996, and 1995. The perch fishery on Lake Vermilion is relatively insignificant, with most of the harvest incidental while targeting other species. There is potential for catching quality sized perch in the Big Bay area of East Vermilion, where 55% of the gillnet catch was 9 inches or longer. The trapnet catch of bluegill was 27.0 fish/net, slightly above the historical average. The bluegill catch was much higher in West Vermilion than in East Vermilion. The mean length of trapnetted bluegill was 5.5 inches, slightly below the historical average. High numbers of small bluegill are present in the population from strong 1995 and 1997 year classes. Angling prospects in 2001 are good, particularly in West Vermilion, although anglers can expect to catch more small fish than usual.The black crappie trapnet catch was 1.4 fish/net, which is near the historical average. Crappie numbers are usually relatively low on Lake Vermilion, although occasional population spikes occur in response to strong year classes. The mean length of trapnetted crappie was 8.5 inches, which is near the historical average. Moderately strong year classes were produced in 1994, 1995, and 1997. Angling prospects in 2001 are similar to recent years. Fair numbers of crappie 8-10 inches long will be available to anglers from the strong 1997 year class.The annual electrofishing assessment of smallmouth bass was not done in 2000 due to poor weather in June. The 1999 electrofishing assessment indicated the population was at a high level with a strong 1997 year class dominating the population.Muskie population assessments are done on Lake Vermilion once every four years for each of the two major lake basins, East Vermilion and West Vermilion. Lake Vermilion is part of the Minnesota Department of Natural Resources (DNR) Large Lake Monitoring Program which includes annual fisheries population assessments, fish disease examinations, water quality monitoring, zooplankton monitoring, aquatic invasive species surveillance, and regularly scheduled creel surveys on the 10 largest lakes in Minnesota. Since 1984, annual fish population assessments on Lake Vermilion have included a variety of sampling gears to collect various fish species at different life stages. These gears include gill nets, trap nets, shoreline seines, and electrofishing boats. Sampling is conducted at the same general time of year and locations for each gear type in order to track population trends. Length, weight, and age data are collected for game fishes of management concern. Lake Vermilion is comprised of two major basins, East Vermilion (area east of Oak Narrows) and West Vermilion (area west of Oak Narrows). An updated management plan for Lake Vermilion was finalized in 2017 to guide fisheries management for a six year period from 2017-2022. Additionally, a new special regulation for walleye came into effect in May 2017. The special regulation for walleye is a 20-26 inch protected slot limit, with one fish over 26 inches allowed in the four fish possession limit. The goal of the regulation is to provide additional harvest opportunity while maintaining safe harvest levels and adequate spawning stock. 2017 Angling Prospects The Lake Vermilion fishery is healthy and should provide both catch and harvest opportunities for multiple species. The walleye population is in good condition in terms of abundance, size, and age distribution. Harvest opportunity is available for walleyes from 13-20 inches, and fish over 20 inches continue to be abundant providing opportunity for a memorable fish. Smallmouth bass abundance continues to be high with fish over 14 inches available. Black crappie, bluegill, largemouth bass, northern pike, and yellow perch all will provide additional angling opportunities. Trophy opportunities exist for muskie anglers as fish over 50 inches are present in the population. Walleye The 2016 annual gill-net survey had a walleye catch rate of 14.0 fish/net which was near the historic average for Lake Vermilion. The average length of walleyes captured was 14.4 inches which was above the historic average. Average length has increased since the implementation of the protected slot in 2006. The catch rate of 13-20 inch walleyes is slightly above the historic median suggesting fish of preferred harvest sizes are available. Additionally, the numbers of fish 19 inches and larger continue to be above historic averages. Walleyes captured in gill nets in 2016 ranged in age from 0 to 15 years. Catch rates of age-0 (2016 year class), 1 (2015 year class), 4 (2012 year class), 5 (2011 year class), and age-8 and older (2001-2009 year classes) fish were above historical averages. As observed in the 2015 survey, the age-4 fish from the 2012 year class continue to persist at numbers well-above average. Walleyes age-8 and older continue to be well represented in the gill net sample representing about 11% of the catch. In the past 10 years, strong year classes were produced in 2007 and 2012 and weak year classes were produced in 2008 and 2009. Preliminary estimates suggest that the 2015 year class is strong. Fall electrofishing provides general information on the abundance and growth of young-of-the-year (YOY) walleyes at or near the end of their first growing season. Both the catch rate of YOY walleyes and the size of fish captured are useful in predicting future year class strength. In 2016, the catch rate of YOY walleyes was 137.0 fish/hour which was slightly above the historic average. The average length of fish captured was 6.1 inches which was the second highest value observed dating back to 1988. Given the gill net catch rate, electrofishing catch rate, and large average size of YOY walleyes sampled, the early indication is that the 2016 year class will be moderate to strong. Yellow Perch The 2016 yellow perch gill net catch rate of 13.9 fish/net was the lowest catch rate ever observed on Lake Vermilion. The highest catch rate ever observed was in 2013, but catch rates have declined since then. Perch catch rates tend to be quite variable from year to year, so it takes multiple years of data to understand trends. The mean length of yellow perch captured in 2016 was 7.7 inches, slightly above the historic average. The catch rate of fish 9 inches and larger showed a modest increase and was the highest observed since 2008. Yellow perch captured in gill nets ranged from 1-6 years old. Northern Pike The 2016 gill net catch rate was 0.2 fish/net which was the lowest catch rate ever observed. Historically, northern pike gill net catch rates have been relatively low and fairly stable ranging between 0.5 and 1.7 fish/net. The catch rates have been trending downward since the late 1980's. Typically, more pike are caught in West Vermilion than in East Vermilion. The annual gill net survey on Lake Vermilion does not target the shallow, vegetated bays where northern pike tend to be found in greater abundance. Additionally, reductions in aquatic vegetation due to rusty crayfish have altered the habitat dramatically, especially in East Vermilion, thus potentially reducing catches in standard gill net sets. A 24-36 inch protected slot limit regulation with one fish over 36 inches allowed in a three fish possession limit for northern pike was implemented in 2003. The regulation change was part of a state-wide initiative to improve the size structure of northern pike populations. There is some evidence in the creel and gill net data that the average size of northern pike has increased following the regulation, but sample size has been low which limits analysis. Information collected from spring ice-out trapnetting in 2017 will be used to assess changes in size structure. The last assessments of this type were done in 1997 and 1998 prior to implementation of the special regulation. Smallmouth Bass The 2016 spring electrofishing catch rate of smallmouth bass was 58.3 fish/hour which was above the 75th percentile for Lake Vermilion. The average length was 10.1 inches, which was near the historical average. Catch rates during spring electrofishing surveys have increased since sampling began in 1989 indicating increased abundance. Typically higher catch rates are observed in West Vermilion but the average size tends to be larger in East Vermilion. Bluegill The 2016 trap net catch rate of bluegill was 16.9 fish/net, which was well below the historical average and the lowest catch rate observed since 2006. Bluegills captured in trap nets had an average length of 5.7 inches, with very few fish captured over 8 inches. Historically, lakewide trap net catches of bluegill have been extremely variable ranging from 14.4 to 64.7 fish/net from 1987 to 2015. Bluegills are more abundant in West Vermilion compared to East Vermilion. Black Crappie The 2016 trap net catch rate of black crappie was 1.1 fish/net, which was slightly below the historical average and down from catches observed in 2014 and 2015. The average length of fish captured was 9.0 inches and the catch was primarily composed of fish in the 9.5 to 11.5 inch range. Black crappie abundance has historically been relatively low and stable on Lake Vermilion with generally higher abundance in West Vermilion. Notable black crappie catches and harvest were reported by anglers in West Vermilion in 2016. Aquatic Invasive Species Aquatic invasive species are not native to Minnesota and cause varying levels of economic and environmental harm. Several invasive species are present in Lake Vermilion including Chinese mystery snails, curly-leaf pondweed, Heterosporis sutherlandae, purple loosestrife, rusty crayfish, and spiny waterfleas. Chinese mystery snails were first discovered in Spring Bay in 2011 and have since been reported in an adjacent bay. Their impact on the lake is unknown but likely negligible. Purple loosestrife has been found at several sites on the lake, usually in wetland areas adjacent to lake. Heterosporis sutherlandae is a microsporidian parasite that infects muscle tissue in fish and causes the disease Heterosporis. Heterosporis has been identified in several walleye and yellow perch from Lake Vermilion, mostly from the west end of the lake. The impact on fish populations is likely negligible. A small, but dense population of curly-leaf pondweed was first surveyed in Everetts Bay in 2009. Since then, annual surveys have been conducted and curly-leaf pondweed has not reached nuisance levels. The plant has been found in Stuntz Bay at low levels as well. Control and removal techniques have been evaluated and used sporadically with varied success. The curly-leaf pondweed infestations are often intermingled with native aquatic vegetation and there is a concern that increased herbicide treatments could reduce native plant diversity. Rusty crayfish have been monitored in the gill net catch in the lake since the early 1990's; monitoring shows their numbers peaked between 2011 and 2014 but were down in 2015. However, the 2016 catch was back above average. Rusty crayfish have been more abundant in East Vermilion and have expanded into West Vermilion. Aquatic vegetation has been greatly diminished in areas of the lake that have been colonized. They seem to prefer aquatic vegetation in sandy areas so less impact has been observed in bays with soft bottom substrates. Spiny waterfleas are an invasive zooplankton first discovered in Lake Vermilion in 2015. As of now, spiny waterfleas have only been sampled in East Vermilion. Other large lakes with a longer history of spiny waterflea presence including Rainy Lake, Lake Kabetogama, and Lake of the Woods have seen significant declines in native zooplankton biomass and density following the introduction of the invasive zooplankton. Lake users should follow Minnesota's Clean, Drain, Dispose laws to help prevent the spread of aquatic invasive species. Fisheries Management Lake Vermilion is composed of two major basins, East Vermilion (east of Oak Narrows) and West Vermilion (west of Oak Narrows), that are slightly different in terms of habitat and fish communities. Length, weight, age, and other scientific data are collected for fish of management concern. The current management plan for Lake Vermilion was designed to guide fisheries management for a six-year period from 2017 to 2022. Management Summary Lake Vermilion is managed to support a high-quality, multi-species fishery driven largely by strong natural reproduction for most species. The lake is intensively monitored and managed by the Minnesota DNR through long-term annual surveys, periodic creel surveys, stocking programs for Walleye and Muskellunge, ecological monitoring, outreach, and management planning activities. Harvest for most species is regulated using statewide seasons and limits except for Walleye, which has a 4 fish limit with a 20-26-inch protected slot. Northern Pike are managed with the northeast zone regulation that allows a 2 fish limit with a 30-40-inch protected slot. Like many large lakes, Vermilion is dealing with aquatic invasive species. Zebra mussels are now considered established, based on the presence of larvae, even though adult mussels have not been documented. Rusty crayfish are also well established, particularly in East Vermilion, where they have altered habitat by reducing aquatic vegetation. Finally, spiny waterfleas may be encountered especially when trolling. For anglers, this means potential changes in fish location and an increased responsibility to prevent further spread.
